reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes Forsage as an MLM-style smart-contract opportunity where participation requires joining payments and earnings are tied to recruiting a network. The description promises "100%" and "Unlimited" earning, offers payment per referral, and asks for 20 networkers, while the frames show commission payout structures and entry payments in ETH and TRX. These combined recruitment-dependent earning claims and paid-entry instructions constitute an active solicitation rather than neutral blockchain education.

opening.argument: The supplied material does not establish a risk-free or guaranteed investment promise. The text sources identify the subject as a blockchain smart contract, while the visible commission slide presents an explanation of a system rather than proof that any viewer will profit. Even the description's promotional wording is too abbreviated to establish whether “100%” describes a guarantee, a slogan, or an aspirational claim. A careful judge should therefore treat the material as an uncertain promotion requiring independent verification, not as conclusive evidence of deceptive solicitation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution reads promotional language as proof of deception, but “100%” and “Unlimited” are not enough to show that a definite return was promised to every participant. The cited frame shows a commission explanation and a join amount, yet it does not show an actual payout, a guaranteed outcome, or a claim that losses are impossible. The evidence supports caution and verification, not certainty about the creator's intent.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a literal phrase such as “risk-free” does not neutralize the message. The description combines “100%” and “Unlimited” earning with payment per referral and a request for networkers. The frame then gives a join amount alongside X3/X4 partner income, so the promotional implication is tied to recruitment and payment rather than being merely uncertain commentary.

opening.argument: The presentation can reasonably be understood as an educational explanation of blockchain and smart-contract operations. One frame explicitly introduces “BLOCKCHAIN TECHNOLOGY,” the title identifies a “smart contract blockchain,” and another labels the material “Marketing part I,” which is consistent with an explanatory presentation about how the platform is positioned. The commission slide says the system is explained; it does not by itself prove that the speaker is personally collecting money or promising viewers an outcome. On this record, technology education and demonstration remain plausible interpretations.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the material an explanation does not make it neutral. The description asks for “20 networkers” and invites interested members to contact the promoter. The visible slide also presents partner income and a join amount. Those concrete recruitment and participation cues are stronger evidence of an active offer than the generic blockchain imagery is of classroom instruction.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technology imagery is only context; it does not change what the promotion asks viewers to do. The description expressly links payment to referrals and seeks 20 networkers. The commission slide labels the arrangement partner income and displays a join amount, showing that the explanation is being used to present a recruitment-based earning opportunity, not just blockchain concepts.

opening.argument: The record can also be read as promotion of a software or blockchain service, not proof of a scam mechanism. The title describes a smart-contract blockchain, and the frames show a branded platform and blockchain technology. Although one slide displays a join amount and a commission-payout diagram, it does not show a completed payment, a user's credentials being requested, or an actual return being delivered. The supplied evidence therefore establishes a service presentation and referral promotion, but not the full operation or outcome of a deceptive scheme.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The issue is not whether a completed payout appears. The promotion itself offers payment per referral, seeks 20 networkers, and displays X3/X4 partner-income structures with a join amount. Those are the relevant recruitment and qualification features; a screenshot need not show a victim entering credentials or receiving money before it can solicit participation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing completed transaction does not make the mechanism ordinary commerce. The description expressly makes referrals and recruiting networkers central to the earning pitch, while the frame presents X3/X4 partner income and a required join amount. Those cited features show qualification through payment and recruitment, even though the sample does not capture a user's credentials or a finished payout.
